messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: Enquiry about BioGeoBEARS
parts:
Some questions from someone beginning an analysis:

> 
> On Thu, Nov 13, 2014 at 10:37 PM, Qin Li <qin...@biodiversity.ubc.ca> wrote:
> 
> 1) the current phylogeny across the genus (~80 taxa) is reconstructed with three
> genes from specimen samples, therefore most species only had one sample and a few (~
> 8 taxa) had more than one. The sampling for taxa is definitely not across the whole
> distribution range. But I saw somewhere you mentioned that this sampling strategy is
> not fit for the range evolution modeling since one specimen can only occur in one
> area at one time (which cannot represent the range of the species).


So, the key thing here is that your OTUs represent species or monophyletic populations. It is (reasonably) OK to use one specimen to establish the phylogenetic position of a species, but you would want to use the geographic range of the species (e.g. from a monograph or field guide or GBIF data or whatever), rather than the geographic range of just that specimen.  If some species are represented by multiple specimens, you would want to reduce that species down to a single tip for the purposes of the BioGeoBEARS analysis.  See:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#no_specimen_trees

...of course, all of this depends on the coarseness of your regions -- with coarse regions, in many cases the species ranges and specimen ranges will be effectively the same (present in coarse region A, absent in coarse region B).


 
> 2) there are genetic data from next-generation sequencing for one clade in this
> genus (5-10 samples across the range for each speces), so there could be extra
> genome-wide inference to estimate historical demography. But the question is there
> is only 10 taxa in this clade. And i wonder if it’s a small sample size to work with
> this clade instead of the whole genus phylogeny.

You should just make a best-guess at what the species/monophyletic populations are, given the data at hand, and then mention this decision and its limitation in your manuscript.

Re: 10 taxa, that is pretty small.  You may have difficulty getting statistically significant differences between models (e.g. DEC vs. DEC+J), but sometimes that's not the main goal.  You can still use the ancestral range inferences etc. like you would as usual.


> 3) Since the study systems in historical geography papers I read are island systems> or across continents with some influential geological events (which had big impact
> on biota), I wonder if I could work on this genus of which most species are
> distributed within a continental scale. The problems I thought would be:
> 
> a. the definitions of areas. Right now I am thinking to do it based on ecoregions.
> But there are more problems. For example, many species in this genus are distributed
> in Serria Nevada mountains in California with different locations and different
> range sizes, and there will be no distinction if I treat Serria Nevada to be one
> area. But if I divide this region into many areas, is it an issue that areas in this
> method are with different resolution (compared to areas: southern California
> mountain area, sonoran desert, Great basin area)?


Determination of the discrete areas is the big subjective step in almost any analysis.  All I can say is that (A) you can't have too many areas, due to the state-space problem (see previous message on this google group), and (B) try to make your areas "evolutionarily meaningful", e.g. areas coarse enough that geographic range is changing slowly on the phylogeny. Another way of saying this is that your best bet is to chose areas at a coarse enough scale that geographic range (the areas occupied) shows some conservation on the phylogeny -- if a lineage is moving in and out of an area every 10,000 years, and the branch lengths on the tree are each say > 1 million years, then those areas aren't meaningful at the phylogenetic timescale.

Using ecoregions is a common choice for within-continent analyses, probably they are often more meaningful, due to migrations as a result of glacial periods etc.  You can feel free to merge ecoregions if needed, or elevations or whatever. Sometimes people do e.g. one analysis with elevation zones as areas, and another with, say, ecosystem type (grassland, forest, etc.). It may be that some of these show more conservation than others.


> b. many sister species have great asymmetry in their current range size, this info> might be lost if we had a small number of areas (they occur in the same area but
> actually they have different range size in this area).
 
That's a tough one.  If the small areas are effectively islands (e.g. mountaintops), it makes reasonable sense to treat them as separate evolutionary areas.  If the range is small due to narrow ecological range, some kind of continuous, SDM approach might be better.  If it's something else (being out-competed by the sister species, human causes), there probably isn't a statistical model yet, and all you can do is think about it and make a verbal argument.  Which is fine of course.



> c. the historical geology and climate oscillation might play an important role on
> distribution change/evolution in Western Norther America. However, there is no
> fossil record or other extra information to estimate the real divergence time for
> this phylogeny. So I am not sure how to evaluate the applicability to use this
> method without information to justify the parameters (ie. dispersal) under complex
> historical impacts.

Well, with only 10 species and with limited information for dating, you will be pretty contrained in what you can do.  Complex models require lots of data. It's perfectly fine to do a simple analysis, and wait for more data in the future to do more complex analyses. 

If you have geographic data from GBIF or collecting, you could do an SDM of each species and then try to look at niche overlap, niche evolution, etc. The methods here are pretty crude (I've just gotten a grant to work on integrating SDMs, historical biogeography, and niche evolution -- people interested in collaborating should email me!), but they can indicate at least e.g. big niche shifts.



> 4) another goal for me to apply this method is to explore the geographical pattern> of speciation, whether sympatric or allopatric one is more common in  this system.

This may be hard with only 10 species.  That's basically 10 data points, and only 9 speciation events, some of which may be ambiguously reconstructed. Still, it would tell you one thing if all the sister species are (A,AB) vs. e.g. (A, B).


> But definitely it’s related to the way in which I define the areas before modeling.
> However, I wonder if I could create several alternative null models with different
> speciation scenarios with BioGeoBEARS, i.e. model 1 with allopatric speciation with
> equal range split, model 2 with sympatric speciation, model 3 with allopatric
> speciation with non-equal range split, etc. Is it practical with parameter settings?

Yes, this part is easy.  But with only 10 species the data likelihoods may not change much between models -- in a typical Hawaii-like situation where everything is a single-island endemic, 10 species might be enough to prefer DEC+J over DEC, but if there are any species occupying more than 1 area, probably the DEC, DIVALIKE, BAYAREALIKE, +J versions, and whatever other models one invents will confer about the same likelihood on the data. You won't know until you try, of course!

If you get serious about this part of it, and can't figure out how to make new models, I can make new custom models, but it's more of a collaboration-type-thing than a free-help-type-thing.

Cheers!
Nick
